scenario_metadata.notes: Illustrative synthetic scenario data. Tariff baseline/spike figures are grounded in real 2025-2026 Section 301 semiconductor tariff policy (25% -> 50% doubling precedent, further escalation actions in motion); all other figures (costs, capacities, transport costs, facility fixed costs) are invented for modeling purposes and are not sourced from real supplier contracts. Demand/capacity/inventory quantities were scaled x10 from the original design-phase values (to move from tens into hundreds/low-thousands) -- per-unit rates (supplier unit cost, tariff %, transport cost per unit, holding cost per unit, backorder cost per unit) were deliberately left UNCHANGED, so all previously-verified hand-worked test cases and the network design decision (F1, F3, F4 open) remain structurally identical, just at 10x dollar/unit magnitude.

demand_generation_methodology.description: Both historical_demand_last_8_weeks and actual_demand_ground_truth_by_week are generated the same way: weekly_demand (the fixed baseline) multiplied by a noise factor drawn from a uniform distribution on [0.5, 1.5] (i.e. +/-50%, widened from an initial +/-20%), rounded to a whole unit. The demand-spike disruption (week 6, C5, x1.5) is layered multiplicatively on top of this noise for that specific customer-week only. Generated ONCE via a seeded random process, then frozen -- identical for every participant and every forecasting method, exactly like the disruption schedule. Actual demand is intentionally generated independently of any forecasting method's prediction: forecasting methods are scored on how well they predict this fixed, pre-existing ground truth from historical data alone, not the other way around. This preserves comparability across participants and keeps the solve-once-per-forecasting-method Oracle architecture valid, since every method faces the same underlying reality. Note: widening the noise band to +/-50% was found NOT to be sufficient on its own to produce backorders against an Oracle-quality (full 4-week-lookahead) decision-maker -- the checkpoint-based ordering discipline is structurally robust to demand noise regardless of magnitude, within reasonable bounds. Backorders were achieved instead by testing a naive, no-lookahead heuristic decision-maker against the same disruption (see hand_worked_test_cases.md, Test Case 6).

network_design_reference_solution.description: Brute-force-verified optimal answer for Stage 0 (Network Design), used as ground truth to validate the Oracle's network design output before trusting it.

runner_up.note: Only $80 more expensive than the true optimum -- intentionally close, so a participant reasoning by intuition could plausibly (and defensibly) land here instead.

per_period_cost_parameters.note: Holding/backorder rates are deliberately stylized/compressed for whole-number player readability within a 10-week horizon; they are not derived from a literal real-world annualized inventory carrying cost percentage. initial_on_hand_inventory_units applies identically to every opened facility at the start of week 1 (before any period-1 decision), same value across facilities like the floor/ceiling. This parameter was missing until hand-worked Test Case 1 revealed that a true zero-inventory cold start is mathematically infeasible: with zero starting stock, the Week-3 checkpoint requires 275 units from the two fastest suppliers combined (Domestic + Regional), but their combined capacity caps out at 270 -- infeasible regardless of cost. 100 units resolves this with comfortable feasibility margin across all three opened facilities (F1, F3, F4) without trivializing the ordering decision.

disruption_schedule.description: Overseas Manufacturer's tariff temporarily escalates from 50% to 100% for this week only, pushing landed cost from $15 to $20 per unit -- temporarily more expensive than Domestic Fab ($18).
C5's demand temporarily increases by 50% for this week only.
Overseas Manufacturer's capacity at every facility is temporarily cut by 50% for this week only.
